title: What Do You Enjoy Doing? The Grammar of Habits and Decisions
paragraphs: Ask someone about their daily life and you will quickly encounter two types of grammar: gerunds and infinitives. "I enjoy running in the mornings." "I've decided to learn Kazakh properly." "She tends to procrastinate." "He can't stand waiting in queues." These structures appear in almost every conversation about habits, preferences, decisions, and intentions.

A gerund is simply a verb that ends in -ing and functions as a noun. "Running is good for you." "Studying takes time." "She loves reading." In each case, the -ing form names an activity — it is the subject or object of the sentence rather than the main verb. Gerunds often feel like habits or general activities. "I enjoy cooking" describes something I do regularly, something I have a general attitude towards.

An infinitive — the "to + base form" structure — often describes something that hasn't happened yet: a plan, an intention, a hope. "She decided to apply." "He hopes to graduate." "They want to travel." The infinitive points forward. It represents what you are trying, hoping, planning, or deciding to do.

The distinction is not always about time, however. "She loves to swim" and "She loves swimming" are both correct, and in casual English they mean essentially the same thing. With many common verbs — like love, hate, prefer, like, begin, start, continue — both forms are acceptable. The real challenge comes with verbs that only take one form.

Verbs that insist on a gerund: enjoy, mind, avoid, miss, consider, practise, admit, deny, imagine, involve, keep, suggest, risk, fancy, finish, delay. "I enjoy to swim" is wrong. "I enjoy swimming." "She denied breaking the window." "He finished studying."

Verbs that insist on an infinitive: want, decide, hope, plan, promise, expect, manage, refuse, agree, afford, offer, fail, tend, learn, need. "I want swimming" is wrong. "I want to swim." "She failed to submit the form." "He agreed to help."

Some verbs take either form, but with a change in meaning. "I stopped smoking" means I no longer smoke. "I stopped to smoke" means I paused what I was doing in order to smoke. "I remember posting the letter" means I have a memory of having done it. "I remember to post the letter" means I won't forget to do it in the future. These differences are small but significant — and they reveal how much work grammar does quietly in the background of communication.

Learning which verbs take which form is largely a question of exposure and practice. There are patterns and there are exceptions. The best approach is to notice how these structures appear in reading and listening, and to practise producing them until they feel natural. And if you make a mistake? Keep trying. Don't stop to worry — just keep working.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: I've decided to start exercising in the mornings. It's been on my list for ages.

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: Oh really? I love training in the mornings. What do you enjoy doing for exercise?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Honestly, I don't mind walking. I can't stand running though.

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: That's fine. Have you considered trying yoga? It's really calming.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: I've thought about it. I keep postponing it, but I plan to start next week.

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: I can help you. I've been practising yoga for two years. I enjoy teaching it too.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Seriously? That would be amazing. I'd really appreciate you helping me.

dialogue.speaker: Zhibek
dialogue.text: It's no problem. Just avoid eating a big meal before the session!

vocab.definition: a verb form ending in -ing that functions as a noun
the base form of a verb, usually with "to"
to keep delaying something that should be done
vocab.example: "She tends to procrastinate." — she keeps delaying things unnecessarily.

vocab.definition: a plan or aim; what you intend to do
vocab.example: "I intend to finish the essay tonight." — intention for the future.

vocab.definition: a clear difference between two things
vocab.example: "The distinction between gerund and infinitive is not always about time."

vocab.definition: the fact of experiencing something; contact with a new experience
vocab.example: "Learning is largely a question of exposure and practice."
Both "She loves to swim" and "She loves swimming" are acceptable.

vocab.definition: important or large enough to be noticed
vocab.example: "These differences are small but significant." — they affect meaning.

task1Items.question: A gerund functions as a ___ in the sentence.
The infinitive often "points ___" — representing plans, hopes, and intentions.
"She loves to swim" and "She loves swimming" mean essentially the ___ .
"Enjoy, mind, avoid, finish" all require the ___ form.
"Want, decide, hope, plan, promise" all require the ___ form.
"I ___ " means I paused what I was doing in order to smoke.
Learning which form to use is mainly a question of ___ and practice.

task2Items.statement: A gerund always acts as the main verb of a sentence.
The infinitive often describes future plans, intentions, and hopes.
"I enjoy to swim" is grammatically correct.
"She loves swimming" and "She loves to swim" are both acceptable.
"I stopped smoking" and "I stopped to smoke" have the same meaning.
"I remember posting the letter" means I have a memory of doing it.
"I want swimming" is a correct English sentence.
The best approach to gerunds and infinitives is exposure and practice.

questions.text: "I stopped ___" means I no longer smoke. (one word)
questions.hint: "I stopped SMOKING" = I no longer smoke. Gerund after "stopped" = the action that ended.

questions.text: What is the difference between "I stopped smoking" and "I stopped to smoke"?
opts: "Stopped smoking" = no longer smokes; "stopped to smoke" = paused to smoke
questions.correct: "Stopped smoking" = no longer smokes; "stopped to smoke" = paused to smoke
questions.hint: Gerund after "stopped" = the action that ended. Infinitive after "stopped" = the purpose of stopping.
